CL

Claude Code

Stale · researched 2026-07-26T08:17:43Z

Characteristics

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: rather than only completing code as it is typed, it independently plans and executes multi-step tasks - reading a project, editing files, running commands and tools, and iterating until a task is verified as done - reporting back rather than requiring per-step confirmation. A single natural-language instruction can produce runnable code across multiple files in one operation, extending to instruction-driven, multi-file refactors where a documented pattern has a primary agent locate every affected call site and delegate the same replacement to a sub-agent per file. When something fails, Claude Code documents running a test or build command, detecting failures, and iterating on fixes within a single continuous turn, without requiring a new prompt between attempts.

Before edits are written, Claude Code offers upfront plan review: a dedicated 'plan' permission mode routes file-edit and shell-write calls to a review callback, and a distinct ExitPlanMode tool presents the assembled plan for explicit approval before autonomous execution begins. Individual edits are then shown as a side-by-side diff the user can accept, reject, or redirect before it is written to disk, and a native checkpoint/rewind mechanism (/rewind, or Esc-Esc) automatically snapshots code state before every prompt so the user can restore code and conversation together to an earlier point. A hooks system spans the agent's action lifecycle (PreToolUse/PostToolUse and other session events); notably, a PreToolUse hook can deny a tool call even in bypassPermissions mode, letting an organization enforce policy the user cannot bypass simply by switching autonomy mode.

For large or long-running work, Claude Code documents an automatic conversation-compaction mechanism that triggers before the context window fills, plus vendor guidance for monorepos such as running an LSP server for symbol-based search and maintaining a lightweight codebase map. Two persistence mechanisms distinguish it from a stateless assistant: layered CLAUDE.md instruction files at personal, project, and enterprise-managed scope, applied through a documented, fixed precedence order, and an 'auto memory' mechanism where Claude writes and persists its own notes based on user corrections across sessions. Work can be decomposed across agent instances: a user can author custom subagents as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter defining scoped tools, a permission mode, and optional MCP servers, which the main agent delegates to and which a lead agent can also coordinate in parallel by assigning subtasks and merging results, alongside fully independent, concurrently running sessions via git worktrees, separate tabs, or multiple simultaneous cloud invocations.

Some capabilities found in adjacent tools are not documented for Claude Code. No official source describes a built-in, embedding-based semantic search across the whole codebase - Claude Code's own documentation instead frames grep/glob-based 'agentic search' as a deliberate design choice. No as-you-type ghost-text or inline code completion is documented in any IDE extension. And no fully offline/air-gapped operating mode or supported local/self-hosted model backend is documented; Claude Code always requires reaching a model-serving endpoint, whether Anthropic's own API or a customer's Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry account.

Access methods

Claude Code's primary interface is a full-featured, standalone terminal CLI that supports editing files, running commands, and managing an entire project directly from the command line, independent of any IDE. Native extensions bring the same functionality into two officially supported IDE families - VS Code (and forks) and JetBrains IDEs. A print/headless mode (-p/--print) supports fully non-interactive, scripted invocation with structured JSON output and documented non-zero exit codes on error, and the product documents CI/CD integration via GitHub Actions and GitLab.

A browser-based 'Claude Code on the web' product lets a user connect a GitHub repository and delegate coding tasks that run on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure without local installation, and a dedicated 'Code' tab in the official Claude app for iOS and Android lets users start, monitor, and steer sessions - reaching cloud sessions or a session on their own machine via Remote Control - directly from a phone.

For enterprise deployment, Claude Code can run through a customer's own Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry account rather than only Anthropic's shared multi-tenant cloud, integrating with the customer's own IAM, audit logging, and VPC configuration; both Bedrock and Vertex additionally support VPC Service Controls/endpoints that keep model traffic entirely within the customer's private network. Region selection for data storage and model inference is documented as configurable when deployed this way (an AWS_REGION setting for Bedrock; VERTEX_REGION_<MODEL_NAME> variables or a /setup-vertex wizard for Vertex AI), and Anthropic's platform documentation separately describes configurable 'workspace geo' (data-at-rest/endpoint-processing location) and 'inference geo' (per-request model-inference location) for these cloud-provider deployment paths.

Internal tools and mechanisms

A built-in sandboxed Bash tool provides OS-enforced filesystem and network isolation for shell commands and their child processes, confining them to defined file paths and allow-listed network domains; separately, Claude Code documents enterprise proxy allow-listing/firewall rules for the specific domains it needs, and its reference devcontainer ships an init-firewall.sh script blocking all outbound traffic except explicitly allowed domains. Terminal command execution itself follows a permission-gated model: a built-in set of read-only commands (ls, cat, git status) runs without prompting, while anything that can modify the system requires explicit approval, with sandboxing or auto-accept modes able to further reduce per-command prompts.

Long-running shell processes can be moved to the background (Ctrl+B, or by explicit request) and tracked under a task ID with output written to a retrievable file, so the interactive session is not blocked. On top of this ad hoc backgrounding, a first-party scheduling mechanism supports Desktop scheduled tasks that start a local session automatically at a chosen time or frequency, and cloud 'Routines' with recurring triggers (hourly, nightly, weekly, plus API/GitHub event triggers) that run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure independent of the user's machine.

Permission is not a single global toggle: named modes (default, acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, bypassPermissions) behave differently per action category, and a declarative settings.json permission-rule system separately grants allow/deny/ask decisions per individual tool and pattern, evaluated in a fixed deny-then-ask-then-allow order ahead of the broader mode check. Static-analysis integration rides on the same general-purpose Hooks mechanism described above: a documented PostToolUse hook example lints newly edited TypeScript/JavaScript files with eslint and feeds failures back to Claude, though no specific linter ships built in by default.

Workflows and use cases

Claude Code documents generating commit messages from staged and unstaged changes and carrying out branch creation and pull-request creation as part of a single guided, conversational workflow rather than only suggesting git commands as text. The dedicated GitHub Actions integration documents Claude opening pull requests directly, with read & write permissions granted specifically to create PRs and push changes, and the same integration provides a GitHub Code Review feature that posts automatic reviews on every PR without a manual trigger, alongside on-demand review via an @claude mention.

Claude Code accepts images - screenshots or design mockups - as prompt input, pasted directly into the CLI or given as a file path, and its documented use cases include generating CSS to match a design mockup, producing new code derived from visual input rather than only describing the image. Documented common workflows also include writing tests that match a project's existing style and frameworks, and instruction-driven, multi-file refactors, including a documented pattern for large-scale refactors (for example, deprecating a function used across dozens of files) where a primary agent locates every call site and delegates the same replacement to a sub-agent per file. Within a single turn, Claude Code can run a test or build command, detect failures, and iterate on fixes without a new prompt between attempts.

Integrations

Claude Code connects to external tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), described in Anthropic's own documentation as reaching 'hundreds of external tools and data sources,' with pre-built servers available for systems like Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres, and Puppeteer. Anthropic's official integration documentation separately lists issue-tracker/monitoring integrations (for example Sentry, via MCP) and a dedicated GitHub Actions integration for CI-driven PR creation and review handling, together spanning multiple named third-party integration categories rather than only one or two.

Beyond connecting external MCP servers, the Claude Agent SDK documents a distinct, in-process custom-tool-authoring surface - the tool() helper in TypeScript, or the @tool decorator in Python - that lets a developer register a function-based tool without configuring or running a separate MCP server process, even though it is wrapped under the hood using the MCP protocol in-process via createSdkMcpServer/create_sdk_mcp_server.

Security

Claude Code's security documentation states user prompts and model outputs are encrypted in transit via TLS 1.2+ and that stored data is encrypted at rest by default. Organization-level access can be governed through SSO/domain capture, role-based permissions, and managed policy settings under Claude for Enterprise, plus Workload Identity Federation for short-lived OIDC-token authentication from identity providers including Okta and Microsoft Entra ID. Two admin-facing oversight surfaces are documented: a Compliance API giving Enterprise customers programmatic access to an audit-level activity feed (SSO events, API-key lifecycle, console activity), and a Claude Code Analytics API providing aggregated daily usage metrics for developer-productivity reporting.

On data retention, Zero Data Retention is documented for Claude Code - prompts and responses are processed in real time and not stored afterward - but it is explicitly excluded from the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and requires separate, per-organization enablement by Anthropic rather than a self-service admin toggle; outside ZDR, retained commercial data is documented as never used for model training without express permission. Anthropic's Data Processing Addendum, automatically incorporated into its Commercial Terms of Service, extends to Claude Code usage on Team, Enterprise, and API plans, and itemizes sub-processors in a dedicated schedule with a documented advance-notice mechanism before new ones are added. Anthropic's Commercial Terms also include an IP indemnification commitment covering paying commercial customers against copyright-infringement claims arising from authorized use, though no official source documents an accompanying filter that blocks code suggestions matching public or open-source code.

On code-security tooling, Claude Code's /security-review and 'Claude Security' capability surfaces dependency-vulnerability findings as one of several categories (alongside SQL injection, XSS, and authentication flaws) in an LLM-driven review that Anthropic's own guidance positions as complementary to, not a replacement for, dedicated deterministic dependency-scanning tools; no official page names a specific vulnerability database or enumerates covered package ecosystems. No official source describes an automatic, built-in mechanism that detects and redacts likely secrets or credentials in a prompt, file, or output before it reaches the model or disk; the generic Hooks system could be used to build such a check, but no first-party secret-detection feature ships out of the box.

This summary reflects vendor documentation only and is not legal advice; teams with specific GDPR, data-residency, or contractual DPA requirements should confirm current terms with Anthropic and consult Legal/the Data Privacy Officer before relying on it for a compliance decision.

Constraints

Several capabilities are gated by plan, license, or deployment path rather than being universally available: SSO, domain capture, and role-based permissions are documented specifically under Claude for Enterprise; Zero Data Retention requires a qualified Enterprise account with separate enablement by Anthropic's account team rather than a standard admin toggle; and the IP indemnification commitment applies to paying commercial customers (Team, Enterprise, API) rather than free users. Enterprise/private deployment is achieved through a customer's own Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry account (optionally with a self-hosted gateway), rather than a vendor-provided, fully air-gapped on-premises product, and native region selection for data storage/inference is documented only for those cloud-provider deployment paths, not the default Anthropic-hosted path.

Some mechanisms require additional setup: automated PR review and PR creation depend on installing the Claude GitHub App and its GitHub Actions workflow, or the equivalent GitLab CI/CD integration; static-analysis/lint feedback relies on a user-configured Hooks pipeline, since no linter ships bundled by default; and most third-party MCP integrations require explicitly adding the relevant MCP server. A PreToolUse hook that returns a 'deny' decision blocks a tool call even in bypassPermissions mode, but ordinary PostToolUse hooks can only observe and react to an already-completed action, not undo it.

Several areas fall short of a full match against documented capability: native codebase search is grep/glob-based 'agentic search' rather than built-in embedding-based semantic search, and dependency-vulnerability findings come bundled inside a broader LLM-driven security review rather than a dedicated, named CVE-database-matched SCA integration. No official source documents as-you-type inline/ghost-text code completion in any IDE extension, a fully offline/air-gapped operating mode, a supported local/self-hosted model backend, or a built-in automatic secret-detection/redaction mechanism - each was checked across documentation, product, changelog, and pricing sources with a consistent negative result.

Features

Code Authoring & Editing

  • Not found Inline code completion
    Re-researched across all four D-009-relevant official source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing) for Claude Code (the CLI/IDE tool, not the Claude API or Claude.ai), specifically distinguishing as-you-type ghost-text/inline completion from Claude Code's documented diff-based edit-proposal workflow and CLI popup autocomplete. Documentation: the official VS Code extension page (code.claude.com/docs/en/vs-code) describes the extension's feature set as a sidebar panel with inline diffs of Claude's own proposed edits, plan mode (review/edit a plan before it is applied), auto-accept-edits mode, checkpoints/rewind, file @-mentions, and slash commands - it does not describe ambient, as-you-type code suggestions generated without an explicit instruction. Product page: claude.com/product/claude-code lists the same mechanics - 'inline diffs, @-mentions, plan review, and keyboard shortcuts' - as its core interaction model, again with no mention of live code completion. Changelog: the official GitHub CHANGELOG.md (anthropics/claude-code) and the docs.claude.com release notes were checked; the only 'autocomplete' entries found are for CLI conveniences - bash-mode history-based Tab completion and slash-command autocomplete - not in-editor code completion as the developer types source code. Pricing: claude.com/pricing's plan-by-plan feature descriptions (Pro/Max/Team access to Claude Code, usage limits, MCP, extended thinking, etc.) contain no inline-completion or autocomplete capability gated by or included in any tier, which is consistent with the capability not existing rather than being plan-restricted. A non-official but corroborating signal was found in the product's own GitHub repository: an open, unresolved feature request, 'Feature request: Inline/tab code completions in VS Code and JetBrains extensions' (issue #45573), explicitly asking Anthropic to add native inline/tab completions to the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, and independent commentary describing Claude Code's IDE extensions as deliberately not offering real-time inline tab-completion (positioning GitHub Copilot or continue.dev as the complementary tool for that purpose). Per protocol this non-official material is used only to corroborate the absence, never as the basis for the status itself, which rests solely on the official documentation, product page, changelog, and pricing sources above showing no such feature. All four relevant source classes were checked with mutually consistent results, no material access errors or unresolved conflicts arose, and no full or partial confirmation was found in any official source, so not_found is recorded per the complete not-found protocol (D-009).
  • Has Natural-language-to-code generation
    Claude Code's official overview documentation states the core workflow of telling Claude what to build in plain English, after which it makes a plan, writes the code, and ensures it works, explicitly framed as building full features from a natural-language description rather than only short snippets; the 'How Claude Code works' page confirms this extends to creating new files and coordinated multi-file output for a single instruction. This directly matches has_criteria at greater than snippet granularity (function/file/multi-file), exceeding the partial_criteria ceiling of short-snippet-only generation.
  • Has Multi-file code generation
    Claude Code's official 'How Claude Code works' documentation states that because Claude reads the whole project, a single instruction (its own example: 'fix the authentication bug') causes Claude to search for relevant files, read multiple files for context, and make coordinated edits across them, and separately that Claude Code creates new files and edits existing ones as part of a single coordinated change. This is a single instruction producing coordinated edits and/or new files across more than one file in one operation, without requiring manual per-file re-invocation, satisfying has_criteria and exceeding partial_criteria.
  • Has Automated refactoring
    Claude Code's official 'How Claude Code works' documentation states that because Claude reads the whole project it can handle complex refactoring tasks, feature tracing, and consistency audits across the entire project structure, not just a single file or symbol. The official agents/subagents documentation further describes an explicit large-scale automated-refactoring pattern driven purely by natural-language instruction: for example, deprecating a function used across dozens of files, where a primary agent locates every call site and dedicated sub-agents perform the same instruction-driven replacement in each file. This is a multi-location, instruction-driven refactor rather than a manual IDE-native refactor command and is not limited to single-symbol renames, satisfying has_criteria and exceeding the partial_criteria ceiling.

  • Has Diff review and selective apply
    Claude Code's official interactive-mode documentation states that when Claude wants to edit a file it shows a side-by-side comparison of the original and proposed change and asks for permission before the change is written, with the user able to accept, reject, or redirect Claude, and even edit the proposed diff content directly before accepting. The official permission-modes documentation and product page corroborate this with distinct modes governing per-edit review (default), batched editor/git-diff review after the fact (acceptEdits), or a no-edit planning-only mode (plan), plus the product page's own description of 'inline diffs' and 'plan review' as core interaction mechanics. This is a reviewable diff with accept/reject controls prior to changes being written to disk, satisfying has_criteria at finer than whole-file granularity (per proposed edit, individually editable), so it exceeds the partial_criteria ceiling.

    Claude Code's official documentation states that images (screenshots, design mockups) can be provided directly as input by pasting into the CLI (Ctrl+V, or Cmd+V on macOS in iTerm2) or by giving an image file path, and its official common-workflows page lists 'getting code suggestions from visual content, such as generating CSS to match a design mockup' as a documented use case alongside describing UI elements and debugging from screenshots. This documents accepting an image/screenshot as prompt input and producing new code (not merely a description or explanation of the image) derived from it, satisfying has_criteria.

Agentic Execution & Runtime

  • Has Autonomous multi-step task execution
    Claude Code runs an agentic tool-execution loop that independently plans and carries out multi-step tasks (file edits, commands, tool calls) from a single higher-level prompt, reporting back on completion rather than requiring per-step confirmation. Anthropic documents extended autonomous operation (working independently for hours on incremental progress) and shows single-prompt examples where Claude plans an approach, edits across multiple files, and verifies the result end-to-end.
  • Has Background / long-running task execution
    Claude Code can move a running Bash invocation to the background (Ctrl+B) or be prompted to start one in the background; the command then runs asynchronously under a tracked task ID with output written to a retrievable file, while the interactive session remains free to handle new prompts rather than blocking on the UI until the command finishes.
  • Has Terminal command execution
    Claude Code executes shell/Bash commands directly on the user's behalf as a core, documented capability (the Bash tool) and uses the output as part of completing tasks. The confirmation model requires explicit approval before commands that can modify the system, while a built-in set of read-only commands (e.g. ls, cat, git status) runs without prompting; sandboxing or auto-accept modes can further reduce per-command prompts.
  • Has Sandboxed / isolated execution environment
    Claude Code ships a built-in sandboxed Bash tool that runs shell commands under OS-enforced filesystem and network isolation, rather than directly and unrestricted on the host, so commands (and their child processes) are confined to a defined set of file paths and network domains.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Parallel independent task execution
    Claude Code documents several first-party mechanisms for running multiple independent tasks concurrently as a supported workflow, not just by manually launching separate app instances: parallel sessions using git worktrees so concurrent edits don't collide, multiple independent tabs/windows each with their own history, and cloud sessions where each `--cloud` invocation runs simultaneously and independently, letting several tasks run at once.
  • Has Self-healing error recovery
    Claude Code documents running a test/build command, detecting failures, and iterating on fixes within a single continuous turn, without a new user prompt between attempts. The officially documented headless example runs the whole test-fix loop from one invocation, and the interactive common-workflows example shows Claude planning an approach, editing across files, running tests, and verifying the result in one pass.
  • Has Agent session checkpoint & rollback
    Claude Code documents a session-wide checkpoint/rewind mechanism (the /rewind command, or Esc-Esc) that automatically snapshots code state before every user prompt and lets the user restore code and conversation together back to an earlier point in one operation, not merely a single file or hunk. Checkpoints persist with the conversation across resumed sessions.
  • Has Scheduled / recurring task execution
    Claude Code provides a native scheduling mechanism distinct from ad hoc background execution: Desktop scheduled tasks start a new local session automatically at a chosen time/frequency, and cloud Routines attach recurring triggers (hourly, nightly, weekly, plus API/GitHub event triggers) to a saved prompt-and-repository configuration that runs on Anthropic-managed infrastructure independently of the user's machine. This is a first-party scheduling feature of the product itself, not merely an external CI cron job invoking the CLI.
    other

Agent Customization & Orchestration

  • Has Multi-agent / sub-agent orchestration
    Claude Code documents delegation of work to sub-agents as a supported mechanism: when a task matches a subagent's description, the main agent delegates to it, and the subagent works independently (its own context window, prompt, tool access, and permissions) before returning results. Documentation further describes spawning multiple agents to work on different parts of a task simultaneously, with a lead agent coordinating work, assigning subtasks, and merging results -- i.e. supported parallel/coordinated multi-agent execution, not merely the user manually running separate sessions. This matches has_criteria.
  • Has User-defined sub-agent roles
    Claude Code documents a file-based, user-authorable custom subagent mechanism: Markdown files with YAML frontmatter stored at the user level (~/.claude/agents/) or project level (.claude/agents/), auto-detected on disk without a restart. Frontmatter fields explicitly include tool-access scoping (tools, disallowedTools), a permission mode, and optional attached MCP servers (mcpServers), alongside the subagent's own prompt/description. This is a documented, supported extension mechanism (not undocumented/experimental) letting the user register a new sub-agent/persona with its own prompt, independent tool scope, and optional MCP attachments, directly matching has_criteria.
  • Has Custom tool / function-calling API
    The Claude Agent SDK (which underlies Claude Code) documents a dedicated 'custom tools' authoring surface, separate from its MCP-server-connection page: a developer defines a tool's name, handler, input schema, and description via the tool() helper (TypeScript) or @tool decorator (Python). This does not require configuring or running a separate/external MCP server process; the resulting tool is wrapped with createSdkMcpServer/create_sdk_mcp_server and runs in-process inside the calling application. Because the documentation presents this as a distinct, native registration surface (a function/handler definition, not an external server integration) and Claude calls the registered function directly, it matches has_criteria for a mechanism independent of connecting an external MCP server, even though it is implemented under the hood using the MCP protocol in-process.
    other platform_or_ide
  • Has Agent lifecycle hooks
    Claude Code documents a native hooks mechanism spanning the agent's action lifecycle generally (not a single narrow event): hooks fire around tool calls (PreToolUse/PostToolUse) as well as other session events, and are evaluated as an explicit step in the permission pipeline (PreToolUse Hook -> Deny Rules -> Allow Rules -> Ask Rules -> Permission Mode Check -> canUseTool Callback -> PostToolUse Hook). Critically, a PreToolUse hook can return a permission decision of 'deny' that blocks the tool call before it executes, and this block applies even in bypassPermissions mode or with --dangerously-skip-permissions, i.e. the user cannot simply switch autonomy mode to escape it. This is a documented, user-supplied-logic mechanism that can influence/block an agent action around tool calls broadly, matching has_criteria and exceeding the partial_criteria ceiling of a single narrow event type.
    other
  • Has Permission / autonomy-level granularity
    Claude Code documents multiple independently configurable autonomy levels rather than one global toggle: named permission modes (default, acceptEdits, plan, dontAsk, bypassPermissions) that behave differently per action category -- e.g. acceptEdits auto-approves file-edit operations while Bash commands and other non-filesystem tools still require normal permission prompts. Layered on top of the mode, a declarative settings.json permission-rule system grants allow/deny/ask decisions per individual tool (Bash, Read, Edit, WebFetch, MCP, and others) and per specifier/pattern, evaluated in a fixed deny-then-ask-then-allow order ahead of the broader mode check. This is well beyond a single global confirm/auto-run switch and directly matches has_criteria (at least two independently configurable permission levels covering different action categories).
    other
  • Has Plan visibility before execution
    Claude Code documents a dedicated 'plan' permission mode in which file-edit and shell-write tool calls are routed to a review callback so no writes execute while planning; when Claude finishes planning, it calls a distinct ExitPlanMode tool that presents the assembled plan and explicitly asks the user to approve it before Claude leaves plan mode and begins autonomous execution of the plan's steps. This is an upfront, whole-plan review step gating the start of autonomous execution (not merely a post-hoc diff of completed changes), matching has_criteria.
    other

Context & Code Quality

  • Not found Codebase-wide semantic search
    No official Anthropic source documents a built-in, meaning-based (embedding/semantic) search across the whole Claude Code codebase; the vendor instead documents a deliberate design choice against maintaining any such index. Anthropic's own blog on large codebases states Claude Code 'navigates a codebase the way a software engineer would: it traverses the file system, reads files, uses grep to find exactly what it needs, and follows references across the codebase,' and explicitly contrasts this with RAG-style approaches: 'RAG-powered AI coding tools work by embedding the entire codebase and retrieving relevant chunks at query time... those systems can fail because embedding pipelines can't keep up with active engineering teams... Instead, agentic search avoids those failure modes. There's no embedding pipeline or centralized index to maintain.' The official MCP integration-catalog documentation lists filesystem, GitHub, Context7, Playwright, and Sequential Thinking as featured example servers, with no first-party meaning-based whole-codebase search server. A targeted re-check of the changelog (github.com/anthropics/claude-code CHANGELOG.md and docs.claude.com release notes) surfaced no entry adding semantic/embedding-based codebase search; the only embedding-related hits were unrelated Anthropic cookbook material (VoyageAI embeddings guide, tool-search-with-embeddings notebook, both about a different feature) and open community GitHub feature requests (e.g. issues #28196 and #20836) explicitly asking Anthropic to add local embedding-based semantic search because Claude Code 'currently relies on basic tools like grep and glob' -- itself evidence the capability is not yet shipped. A targeted re-check of the pricing/cost pages (claude.com/pricing, code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) found only usage-cost figures (e.g. per-developer-per-day API spend) and no mention of a semantic-search feature or indexing tier. Third-party MCP servers (e.g. zilliztech/claude-context, community codebase-indexer projects) can bolt on vector-based code search, but per the official-sources-only rule a community integration cannot justify a has/partial status for the vendor's own product. All relevant source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing, integration_catalog, other) were checked via multiple independent queries with consistent, mutually corroborating results and no conflicting official evidence, so the negative-result protocol is satisfied without any unresolved access gap.
  • Has Large-repository / long-context handling
    Claude Code documents both a repository-scale handling mechanism and a long-conversation handling mechanism: a dedicated official guide for setting up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase (e.g. running an LSP server so search is symbol-based rather than string-based, and adding a lightweight codebase map when directory structure alone is insufficient), plus an automatic conversation-compaction mechanism that triggers before the context window fills (with a documented default threshold and configurable override via environment variables) and a manual /compact command with focus options. This is vendor-documented, codebase- and session-specific handling beyond a bare context-window size figure, satisfying has_criteria.
    other
  • Has Persistent project memory / custom instructions
    Claude Code's official memory documentation describes CLAUDE.md files as a mechanism for persisting project-specific instructions/conventions that are automatically loaded at the start of every conversation without the user re-entering them, plus a separate 'Auto memory' mechanism where Claude itself writes and persists notes based on the user's corrections and preferences across sessions. This is a documented, automatically-applied, cross-session mechanism, satisfying has_criteria.
  • Has Automated test generation
    Anthropic's official explainer page on unit testing documents Claude Code as an agentic coding tool that integrates with the developer's environment and generates, refines, and manages unit tests across frontend and backend codebases on request, targeting the developer's existing stack and conventions. This is a documented, first-party test-generation capability rather than incidental code generation, satisfying has_criteria.
  • Has Automated code review / PR review
    Claude Code's official GitHub Actions documentation describes a dedicated GitHub Code Review feature that posts automatic reviews on every PR without requiring a manual trigger, in addition to on-demand review via an @claude mention in a PR or issue comment. This is a dedicated review workflow producing review comments/suggestions on diffs, not merely ad-hoc chat, satisfying has_criteria. A GitLab CI/CD equivalent is separately documented.
    integration_required
  • Has Static analysis / linting integration
    Claude Code's official Hooks reference documents a lifecycle hook mechanism (e.g. PostToolUse) whose explicit purpose includes enforcing formatting/linting on every file write and feeding a block decision plus a reason back so Claude sees and acts on the result, rather than only displaying lint errors in the editor. Documented examples run a linter (e.g. eslint) after Claude edits a file and surface failures back to the assistant, which is a documented integration whose findings inform the assistant's subsequent output, satisfying has_criteria.
    integration_required
  • Partial Dependency vulnerability scanning (SCA)
    Anthropic's official Help Center article and Claude Code documentation for automated security reviews (/security-review, and the Claude Security plugin) list 'dependency vulnerabilities' -- checks for known issues in third-party packages -- as one of several categories of findings an automated security review surfaces, alongside SQL injection, XSS, authentication flaws, and insecure data handling. This documents some dependency-vulnerability surfacing, satisfying part of has_criteria. However, the same official documentation explicitly frames Claude Security's LLM-driven review as complementary to, not a replacement for, dedicated deterministic 'dependency scanning' (SCA) tooling, and no official page documents integration with a named CVE/vulnerability database or states which package ecosystems/managers are covered. This falls short of a documented CVE-database integration with stated ecosystem coverage, so it is recorded as partial rather than has.
    other
  • Has Layered instruction precedence (personal/repository/organization)
    Claude Code's official documentation describes custom-instruction/settings scopes at the enterprise (managed policy), user/personal, and project/repository levels, with an automatically-applied precedence: the memory documentation states that managed-policy CLAUDE.md files cannot be excluded so organization-wide instructions always apply regardless of individual settings, and the admin-setup documentation states that permissions resolve through four settings sources in a fixed precedence order (enterprise managed policy, command-line flags, project settings, then user settings). This covers at least the personal/repository/organization scopes named in the feature definition with a documented, automatically-applied order, satisfying has_criteria.
    other

Workflow & Ecosystem

  • Has Native git workflow support
    Claude Code's official common-workflows documentation describes it generating commit messages from staged/unstaged changes and carrying out branch creation and pull-request creation as part of a single guided workflow, going beyond merely suggesting git commands as text.
  • Has Pull request creation
    The official GitHub Actions documentation states Claude can create pull requests directly (e.g. from an @claude mention in an issue/PR) and that the integration is granted read & write permissions specifically to create PRs and push changes, i.e. the PR is opened by the tool itself on the hosting platform rather than requiring a manual follow-up step by the user.
    integration_required
  • Has Multi-IDE / multi-editor support
    Claude Code is officially supported, not merely community-plugged, in at least two distinct IDEs: a dedicated VS Code extension and a dedicated JetBrains plugin (covering IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, etc.), in addition to standalone terminal use.
  • Has Standalone CLI access
    Claude Code's official overview and CLI reference document a full-featured command-line interface that provides the product's core functionality (editing files, running commands, managing the project) directly from the terminal, independent of any IDE or GUI.
  • Has Web-hosted / browser access
    Anthropic officially documents 'Claude Code on the web', a browser-based application (at claude.ai/code) that provides core coding functionality - connecting GitHub repositories, describing tasks, and having Claude implement changes and open pull requests - on Anthropic-managed cloud infrastructure, without requiring local installation. This is core product functionality, not merely account/billing management, satisfying the has_criteria.
    release_stage plan_or_license
  • Has MCP / plugin extensibility
    The known official MCP documentation page confirms Claude Code supports the Model Context Protocol as a documented mechanism for connecting external tools and data sources, including pre-built servers for third-party systems, satisfying the has-criteria for a documented extension mechanism.
  • Has Third-party integration catalog
    Anthropic officially documents multiple, distinct third-party integrations for Claude Code, beyond the 1-2 threshold for 'partial'. The Claude Code MCP docs officially document connecting to external issue trackers and monitoring tools (e.g. Sentry, via the Model Context Protocol), and a separate, dedicated GitHub Actions integration page documents CI-system integration for automated PR creation and review-comment handling. Together these span issue-tracker and CI-system integrations named explicitly in the feature definition, so the has_criteria (an official integration catalog/documentation page lists supported third-party integrations) is met.
    integration_required
  • Has Mobile app access
    The official Claude Code mobile documentation describes a dedicated 'Code' tab in the official Claude app for iOS and Android that lets users start, monitor, and steer Claude Code coding sessions from their phone (both cloud-hosted sessions and Remote Control of a session on the user's own machine), which goes beyond a generic responsive web view or account-management-only access.
    plan_or_license
  • Has Headless / non-interactive CI mode
    The official CLI/headless documentation defines a print (-p/--print) mode designed for fully non-interactive, scripted invocation, with a documented --output-format json structured output option and documented non-zero exit-code behavior on error, and the product overview documents CI/CD integration via GitHub Actions and GitLab.
  • Not found Full offline operation
    No official Anthropic source documents Claude Code operating with zero network connectivity for its core functionality. The official enterprise network-configuration documentation states the product must reach api.anthropic.com (or an equivalent Bedrock/Vertex/Azure endpoint) for model inference, MCP servers for tool calls, and target hosts for WebFetch, and describes only proxying/allow-listing that traffic rather than eliminating it; no documentation, product, changelog, or pricing page describes a fully offline or air-gapped operating mode. The official CHANGELOG.md and release notes contain no entry introducing offline/air-gapped support (the only offline-adjacent changelog item concerns a plugin marketplace cache fallback, unrelated to core model connectivity). The pricing/enterprise pages describe deployment through a customer's own Bedrock/Vertex/Azure account, which still requires reaching a model-serving endpoint over the network, not zero-network operation. Two open GitHub feature requests in the product's own repository (asking for 'Complete Offline Installation' and for air-gapped-friendly distribution URLs) further indicate this is a requested-but-unimplemented capability rather than a documented feature. A third-party community project claiming fully offline operation via a locally hosted model is unofficial and, even if taken at face value, would fall under the taxonomy's explicit exclusion for a swappable local model (local_offline_model_support) rather than this feature. All relevant source classes were checked and none surfaced supporting evidence.

Security & Governance

  • Has Enterprise SSO / access control
    Claude Code's enterprise deployment documentation states that Claude for Enterprise adds SSO and domain capture along with role-based permissions and managed policy settings for organization-wide Claude Code configurations. Its Authentication docs additionally describe Workload Identity Federation, letting organizations authenticate to the Claude API using short-lived OIDC tokens from identity providers including Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, and others, plus automatic credential refresh for AWS SSO.
    plan_or_license
  • Partial Data retention / training opt-out controls
    Claude Code documents Zero Data Retention (ZDR): when enabled, prompts and model responses generated during Claude Code sessions are processed in real time and not stored by Anthropic after the response is returned. However, ZDR is explicitly documented as not included in the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be enabled from an organization's own admin settings; it is available only to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic per organization. This matches the partial criterion of an opt-out available only on specific enterprise arrangements rather than a generally available, self-service customer-facing control across tiers. Retained (non-ZDR) commercial data is documented as never used for model training without express permission.
    plan_or_license
  • Has On-premises / private cloud deployment
    Claude Code's official enterprise-deployment documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/bedrock-vertex-proxies, /third-party-integrations, /amazon-bedrock) documents that, in addition to Anthropic's own shared SaaS, Claude Code can be deployed through the customer's own Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry account, integrating with the customer's own IAM, audit logging (AWS CloudTrail / GCP Cloud Audit Logs), and VPC configuration. Both Bedrock and Vertex additionally support VPC Service Controls / VPC endpoints so that model traffic stays entirely within the customer's own private network. This is a documented, first-party-supported deployment option (not a community workaround) giving the customer a dedicated, private-network-isolated instance running inside infrastructure the customer controls, rather than only Anthropic's multi-tenant cloud, which satisfies has_criteria. It is delivered through the customer's own cloud-provider account rather than a literal on-prem data-center install of Anthropic's own software, but the feature's definition explicitly includes 'a dedicated private cloud instance' as qualifying, so this is recorded as has rather than partial.
    integration_required
  • Partial IP indemnity / public-code duplication filter
    Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service include an IP indemnification commitment: Anthropic will defend paying commercial customers against copyright-infringement claims arising from their authorized use of the service and its outputs, paying approved settlements or judgments (with standard carve-outs for policy violations, customer modifications, and combinations with non-Anthropic technology). Claude Code's legal-and-compliance docs confirm Claude Code usage is governed by these Commercial Terms for Team/Enterprise/API customers, so the indemnity extends to Claude Code output on paid plans. No official Anthropic or Claude Code source, however, documents a configurable filter that blocks code suggestions matching public/open-source code; only third-party community discussions of ad hoc manual de-duplication commands/plugins were found, which do not qualify as official confirmation of such a filter. Since only one of the two sub-features (indemnification) is officially documented, this is partial.
    plan_or_license
  • Has Audit logging & usage metrics
    Anthropic exposes two admin-facing surfaces covering Claude Code oversight: the Compliance API, which gives Claude Enterprise customers programmatic access to per-event audit data (SSO sign-ins and authentication events, API key lifecycle, console activity such as member invites and role changes), and the Claude Code Analytics API, which provides aggregated daily usage metrics for organizational adoption/productivity reporting. Claude Code's own enterprise-deployment docs confirm this compliance API access and role-based permissions are part of Claude for Enterprise.
    plan_or_license
  • Not found Local / offline (BYO) model support
    Claude Code's official documentation, product page, pricing/plan page, and changelog were all checked this pass and consistently show that Claude Code supports connecting to alternative model back-ends only through the generic, org-controlled 'LLM gateway' mechanism (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL / ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, code.claude.com/docs/en/llm-gateway, /llm-gateway-connect, /model-config), which is documented for reaching Anthropic's own API or Anthropic-hosted models on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry via a customer's own enterprise gateway. That same official gateway page states verbatim, reproduced consistently and independently across multiple searches this session: "Anthropic doesn't endorse, maintain, or audit third-party gateway products, and doesn't support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway." Claude Code's official product page (claude.com/product/claude-code) and model/plan documentation (claude.com/pricing; support.claude.com's Claude Code model-configuration article) list only Anthropic's own hosted Claude models (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) as selectable per plan, with no mention of a supported local or self-hosted (BYO) model option. The official changelog/release-notes sources (github.com/anthropics/claude-code CHANGELOG.md, docs.claude.com/en/release-notes/claude-code) show no entry announcing local-model or Ollama support. Since January 2026, Ollama has shipped its own Anthropic Messages API compatibility layer (per Ollama's own blog/docs, e.g. ollama.com/blog/claude, docs.ollama.com/integrations/claude-code), which lets users point Claude Code's generic gateway environment variables at a locally-run Ollama model; this is corroborated only by Ollama's own (non-Claude-Code) official documentation and numerous third-party tutorials, never by any Anthropic/Claude Code official source, and Anthropic's own documentation explicitly disclaims supporting this use. This does not meet has_criteria (no vendor-documented, supported way to connect a customer's own local/self-hosted model) or partial_criteria (no first-party-endorsed narrower subset either); it is an unendorsed community workaround riding on a generic gateway mechanism built for other purposes. All source classes with plausible coverage (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing) were checked this session and yielded a consistent, on-topic, mutually corroborated negative result -- the exact non-support disclaimer was independently reproduced across separate searches of the same official page -- so not_found (not uncertain) applies with no residual access gap.
  • Not found Secret detection & redaction
    Claude Code's official documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/security), product page (claude.com/product/claude-code), pricing/plan page (claude.com/pricing), changelog/release notes (github.com/anthropics/claude-code CHANGELOG.md, docs.claude.com/en/release-notes/claude-code), and specialist security post (anthropic.com/news/claude-code-security) were all checked this pass. None describe an automatic, built-in mechanism that detects likely secrets/credentials in a prompt, file, or generated output and redacts or blocks them before reaching the model or being written to disk. The official security page documents only secure local storage of Claude Code's own API keys/tokens (OS keychain / file permissions) and a general permission-gated file/command-access model requiring user approval for sensitive operations -- it does not describe scanning user content for embedded secrets. Anthropic's own 'Claude Security' / '/security-review' capability (anthropics/claude-code-security-review, covered in the specialist post) is a static, on-demand vulnerability-scanning review of pending code changes that can incidentally flag hardcoded secrets as one of several finding categories; it is not an automatic interception/redaction control that runs on every prompt or output. Claude Code does ship a generic, official hooks extensibility system (e.g. UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse) that a customer can wire up with their own regex/secret-matching logic to build custom redaction, but this is a general-purpose extension point documented for many uses, not a shipped, Anthropic-authored secret-detection feature in itself, so it does not satisfy has_criteria or partial_criteria on its own. This is corroborated by open, unresolved feature requests on Claude Code's own official GitHub issue tracker (anthropics/claude-code issues #29434 'Mechanism to redact secrets/PII from the context window', #32733 on secure secrets injection for Claude Code on the web, #29910 on built-in secrets management), confirming this remains a documented product gap rather than a released capability; the mechanisms currently filling it (community redaction-hook projects, third-party 'guardrail'/MCP plugins) are not Anthropic's own. All plausible official source classes (documentation, product_page, pricing, changelog, specialist) were checked this session with a consistent, on-topic negative result, so not_found (not uncertain) applies with no residual access gap.
  • Has Agent network egress control / firewall
    Claude Code documents a configurable, non-default network-egress control for its agent execution environment beyond generic process isolation: the sandboxed Bash tool provides filesystem and network isolation and restricts which domains sandboxed processes can reach; the Enterprise network configuration page describes proxy allowlisting and firewall rules for the specific domains Claude Code needs; and the reference devcontainer ships an init-firewall.sh script that blocks all outbound traffic except explicitly allowed domains. Together these describe a configurable allow-list mechanism, not merely a fixed default.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Data processing / residency region control
    Claude Code's own documentation exposes customer-configurable region settings when deployed through a cloud provider: the Amazon Bedrock page documents setting the AWS region (e.g. via the AWS_REGION environment variable / aws_region parameter), and the Google Cloud's Agent Platform (Vertex AI) page documents per-model region/multi-region location settings (VERTEX_REGION_<MODEL_NAME>, plus a /setup-vertex wizard). Anthropic's platform-level data-residency documentation confirms that for AWS Bedrock, Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry deployments both data storage (workspace geo) and model inference (inference geo) can be restricted to a selected geographic region.
    integration_required
  • Has Sub-processor / third-party data-sharing disclosure
    Anthropic's official Data Processing Addendum (anthropic.com/legal/data-processing-addendum), which forms part of Anthropic's commercial contractual terms, itemizes sub-processors in a dedicated Schedule 4 and grants customers a general authorization to engage those listed sub-processors, with a documented advance-notice mechanism (multiple mirrored copies of the DPA text consistently show 15 days' notice) allowing customers to object before any new sub-processor is added. Anthropic separately maintains a dedicated, publicly accessible 'Subprocessors' page on its own Trust Center (trust.anthropic.com/subprocessors) as an apparently live, vendor-maintained disclosure distinct from the contractual DPA schedule. Together these constitute a published, itemized sub-processor list/equivalent disclosure rather than only general privacy-policy language, satisfying has_criteria. This is a legal/contractual matter; anyone with a specific GDPR or Data Processing Addendum requirement for an engagement should confirm current terms directly with Anthropic and consult Legal/the Data Privacy Officer rather than relying solely on this summary.
  • Has Data Processing Agreement (DPA) availability
    Anthropic publishes a Data Processing Addendum (DPA), including Standard Contractual Clauses, that is automatically incorporated into its Commercial Terms of Service; accepting the Commercial Terms of Service also accepts the DPA. Claude Code's own legal-and-compliance documentation states Claude Code usage (via the 1P API, Amazon Bedrock, or Google Cloud's Agent Platform) is governed by those Commercial Terms for Team, Enterprise, and API customers, so the DPA extends to Claude Code for those plans.
    plan_or_license
  • Has Encryption in transit & at rest
    Claude Code's security documentation explicitly states user prompts and model outputs are encrypted in transit via TLS 1.2+, and that stored data (in Google Cloud Storage) is encrypted at rest by default, covering both required aspects of this feature.

Additional facts

Built-in tools

  • Bundled tooling:

    Claude Code does not ship a bundled code formatter or linter by default. Static-analysis/lint feedback is delivered through the general-purpose Hooks mechanism instead: a documented example wires a PostToolUse hook to run eslint against newly edited TypeScript/JavaScript files and feed failures back to Claude, but the user must configure both the hook and the underlying linter/formatter themselves.

    • “A PostToolUse hook can lint new TypeScript/JavaScript files by checking the file extension and running eslint with max-warnings set to 0.”
  • Multi-agent orchestration:

    Claude Code documents more than one concurrency pattern beyond single-subagent delegation: a lead agent can spawn multiple subagents to work on different parts of a task simultaneously, assigning subtasks and merging their results, while separately a user can run fully independent parallel sessions - via git worktrees so concurrent edits don't collide, separate tabs/windows, or multiple simultaneous --cloud invocations, each running as its own independent cloud session.

    • “You can spawn multiple Claude Code agents that work on different parts of a task simultaneously, with a lead agent coordinating the work, assigning subtasks, and merging results.”
    • “Each `--cloud` command creates its own cloud session that runs independently, and you can start multiple tasks that will all run simultaneously in separate sessions.”
  • Named sub-agents:

    Custom subagents are defined as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, stored at the user level (~/.claude/agents/, available across all projects) or the project level (.claude/agents/, shareable with a team), and are auto-detected on disk without a restart. Frontmatter fields scope each subagent independently, including its own tool access (tools, disallowedTools), permission mode, and optionally attached MCP servers.

    • “Subagents are stored as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in two locations: User subagents in ~/.claude/agents/ (available across all projects) and project subagents in .claude/agents/ (specific to your project and shareable with your team).”
    • “The frontmatter fields available include: description, prompt, tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, mcpServers, hooks, maxTurns, skills, initialPrompt, memory, effort, background, isolation, and color.”

Pricing & licensing

  • Plans and availability:

    Some governance-oriented capabilities are restricted specifically to Claude for Enterprise rather than being available across all paid tiers: SSO/domain capture, role-based permissions, and managed policy settings for organization-wide configuration are documented under Claude for Enterprise, and Zero Data Retention is explicitly excluded from the standard Enterprise plan - it requires separate, per-organization enablement by Anthropic rather than a self-service admin setting.

    • “Claude for Enterprise adds SSO and domain capture, role-based permissions, compliance API access, and managed policy settings for deploying organization-wide Claude Code configurations.”
    • “Zero Data Retention (ZDR) for Claude Code is available to qualified accounts on Claude for Enterprise... ZDR is not included in the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be enabled from your admin settings. It is available to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic.”

Security & data handling

  • Data usage:

    Commercial (Team, Enterprise, API) Claude Code usage carries a documented standard 30-day data retention period, with zero data retention available given appropriately configured API keys. Organizations separately get a Compliance API activity feed giving audit-level visibility into SSO sign-ins, API-key lifecycle, and console activity, and Anthropic's Data Processing Addendum grants customers a general, advance-notice-backed authorization to engage the sub-processors it itemizes in a dedicated schedule.

    • “For commercial users (Team, Enterprise, and API): the standard retention period is 30 days, and zero data retention is available with appropriately configured API keys—Claude Code will not retain chat transcripts on servers.”
    • “The Compliance API gives Claude Enterprise customers programmatic access to their organization's Activity Feed... security and compliance teams can monitor SSO sign-ins and authentication events, track API key lifecycle, audit console activity including member invites and role changes, and investigate Claude usage at the audit level.”

cursor

Stale · researched 2026-07-26T09:30:03Z

Characteristics

Cursor is an AI-native coding assistant built by Anysphere, delivered primarily as a fork of Visual Studio Code but increasingly available as a family of first-party surfaces: the desktop editor, a standalone terminal agent (Cursor CLI), an official JetBrains integration via the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), a web application at cursor.com/agents, and a native iOS app. At its core, Cursor pairs an inline, ghost-text autocomplete ('Tab') with a general-purpose, autonomous Agent that can search a codebase semantically, edit multiple files, run terminal commands, and carry out multi-step programming tasks from a single natural-language instruction. Beyond the local, foreground Agent, Cursor documents Cloud Agents that execute asynchronously in isolated VMs (including a Self-Hosted Pool option that keeps tool execution inside a customer's own infrastructure while orchestration and model inference remain in Cursor's cloud), subagents that a parent agent can delegate scoped work to, and dedicated built-in agents such as Bugbot (automated PR review with Autofix) and the paired Security Reviewer / Vulnerability Scanner. The product also documents Plan Mode (an upfront, editable plan before execution begins), session Checkpoints (full-session rollback of Agent-made changes), and persistent Rules/Memories that carry project- and team-level context across sessions without the user re-entering it.

Access methods

Cursor is reachable through several first-party surfaces rather than a single client. The primary surface is Cursor's own VS Code-fork desktop editor. A standalone command-line agent (Cursor CLI / cursor-agent) runs the same agent capabilities in a terminal without any IDE, including an interactive Shell Mode and a non-interactive, scriptable print mode (-p/--print) with JSON/stream-JSON output for CI and automation. Cursor is also officially available inside JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, and others) via the Agent Client Protocol, installed from the ACP Registry and authenticated with an existing Cursor account. A web application at cursor.com/agents provides core agent functionality - writing code, running background agents, reviewing diffs and PRs - from any desktop, tablet, or mobile browser with no local installation required (an installable PWA is offered only as an optional convenience). A native iOS app (public beta, on all paid plans) gives direct assistant access from a phone, including launching and controlling agents, voice input, model selection, and reviewing/merging PRs; no official native Android app was found, so Android access currently relies on the web dashboard or installing the web app as a PWA. For teams building custom, programmatic agent applications, Cursor also ships a Cursor Agent SDK (TypeScript and Python) that exposes the local agent loop, custom tool registration, and cloud-agent orchestration as an API surface distinct from the standard IDE chat UI.

Internal tools and mechanisms

Cursor's agent draws on several documented internal mechanisms rather than a single monolithic model call. Codebase context is built from a semantic indexing pipeline that splits files into syntactic chunks, converts them into cached embeddings, and reuses near-identical existing indexes across a team's highly similar codebase copies to keep large-repository indexing fast and current. A 'shadow workspace' mechanism runs a proposed edit in a hidden window and feeds the running language server's lint diagnostics back into the edit loop before the change is finalized. Execution autonomy is layered rather than a single global switch: file edits apply without approval by default (except configuration files, which still require approval), terminal/shell commands require approval by default but can be governed by a separate Run Mode (an allowlist, an Auto-review LLM classifier, or Run Everything) configured in permissions.json, and MCP tool calls are gated by their own, independent approval setting. A native hooks mechanism (.cursor/hooks.json, repo-scoped, or ~/.cursor/hooks.json, user-scoped) lets an admin or user intercept lifecycle events - before/after shell execution, before/after file edit, pre/post tool use, subagent start/stop, and pre-compact - and return an allow/deny/ask decision or block the action outright. Custom subagents can be authored as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter under .cursor/agents/, each scoping its own tools (or a coarse read-only flag), disallowed tools, MCP servers, hooks, max turns, and skills.

Workflows and use cases

Documented workflows span individual-developer and organizational/CI use. At the individual level, Cursor supports autonomous multi-step coding tasks driven by natural language, inline Tab completions while typing, a dedicated workflow for generating and backfilling unit test coverage, and turning a pasted design mockup image into working UI code via a vision-capable model. Plan Mode supports a research-plan-approve-execute workflow for larger, multi-file changes, with session Checkpoints available to roll back an entire Agent session if it goes wrong. At the team and CI/CD level, the CLI supports headless, scriptable invocation (JSON/stream-JSON output, documented exit codes) for use in GitHub Actions and other automation pipelines; Bugbot automatically reviews every pull request for bugs, security issues, and quality problems, with an Autofix capability that spawns cloud agents to propose fixes; and Automations let a cloud agent run on a cron schedule or in response to events (a GitHub/GitLab PR, a Slack message, a Linear issue, or a generic webhook) without an active user session initiating it. Multiple agents can also run genuinely in parallel, each in its own isolated Git worktree, from the Agents Window, and the built-in Security Reviewer / Vulnerability Scanner agents run on a schedule to flag security issues and outdated dependencies across a codebase.

Integrations

Cursor's primary open extension point is the Model Context Protocol (MCP): MCP servers connect the agent to external tools and data sources (e.g. Google Drive, Notion, databases, other APIs) and are configured consistently across both the editor and the CLI. Cursor operates a vendor-curated Marketplace (cursor.com/marketplace) listing more than 30 third-party integrations from named partners such as Atlassian, Datadog, GitLab, Glean, Hugging Face, monday.com, and PlanetScale, alongside earlier launch partners including Amplitude, AWS, Figma, Linear, and Stripe. For organizations, admins can configure 'Team MCP' servers once and distribute them across cloud agents, the Agents Window, the IDE, and the CLI through a governed Team Marketplace supporting SCIM-group and organization-group-based access control, so individual developers do not need to configure MCP servers themselves. Cursor also documents native Git tooling (AI-generated commit messages, merge-conflict resolution assistance directly from chat, agent attribution, Cursor Blame) and first-party GitHub/GitLab integration for opening pull requests directly from the Agent or Cloud Agents.

Security

Cursor documents a layered security and compliance posture. Enterprise identity and access controls include SAML 2.0 SSO (supporting Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, and other IdPs) with SCIM provisioning and the ability to enforce SSO and disable local login, plus fine-grained RBAC across organizations, teams, and agents; an Audit Log tracks 19 event types and can be exported as CSV. Cloud/background agent execution can be constrained with sandbox network allow-lists (three configurable levels, up to organization-wide enforcement from the admin dashboard) and, for Enterprise customers, a Self-Hosted Pool option that keeps tool execution inside customer-managed infrastructure while orchestration and model inference remain in Cursor's cloud. Cursor's LLM Safety and Controls documentation describes multi-stage secret detection - scanning prompts before submission to the LLM, files before the agent reads them, and generated code before it is written to disk - while also noting these are rules the model is instructed to follow rather than hard guarantees, and recommending they be paired with enforcement hooks. Data protections include AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit, a standing Data Processing Addendum, a publicly itemized sub-processor list, an opt-in 'Privacy Mode' backed by zero-data-retention agreements with model providers, and stated SOC 2 Type II compliance (attestation available on request) alongside GDPR/CCPA compliance. Data residency is US-only by default for inference, processing, and storage, with EU + Iceland inference-only coverage available on request to Enterprise customers and broader regional coverage described as still in development.

Constraints

Several of Cursor's more powerful capabilities are gated to specific plans or deployment modes rather than being universally available. SSO/RBAC, the Audit Log, LLM Safety and Controls (secret scanning), the Security Reviewer/Vulnerability Scanner agents, and Self-Hosted Pool execution are documented as Teams/Enterprise features, not part of the free Hobby or individual Pro tier. Cursor does not document a fully offline or air-gapped operating mode: even the Self-Hosted Pool keeps agent orchestration and model inference in Cursor's cloud, and the officially documented custom-model override (pointing Settings > Models at an OpenAI-compatible base URL - the supported path for self-hosted/local models such as Ollama) still requires a network-reachable endpoint rather than a purely local, disconnected one. Full VM-level sandboxing is documented specifically for Cloud Agents; the default local/foreground Agent runs directly on the user's machine, with only best-effort, per-command shell sandboxing under certain Run Modes rather than a hard security boundary. Data residency is US-only by default, with EU+Iceland coverage limited to inference only and available on request rather than as a self-service, all-region guarantee. IP indemnification is set out in Cursor's Master Services Agreement, which applies to organizations with a negotiated Enterprise agreement rather than to individual Free/Pro subscribers under the standard Terms of Service (where indemnification instead runs from customer to vendor), and is subject to carve-outs such as disabled safety filters or known-infringing use. Native mobile access is currently iOS-only; Android relies on a web dashboard or an installable PWA rather than a dedicated native app. Finally, subagents inherit the parent agent's configured MCP servers/tools by default rather than allowing independent, per-subagent MCP attachment, and registering a custom tool without standing up an MCP server is currently a Cursor Agent SDK capability rather than a setting exposed in the standard IDE chat UI.

Agentic Execution & Runtime

  • Has Autonomous multi-step task execution

This matches the has_criteria of decomposing and executing a task's steps autonomously and reporting back on completion.
  • Has Background / long-running task execution
    Cursor's Cloud Agents run Agent sessions in the cloud, executing asynchronously in an isolated VM without occupying the user's local editor session, and report results back (e.g. via PR comments, dashboard, chat notifications) on completion.   • Has Terminal command execution
    Cursor's Agent documents native terminal command execution with sandboxing, preserved history, and native terminal integration. Commands require user approval by default, but users can configure Run Modes (Auto-review, Allowlist, Run Everything) to change the confirmation model, and Cloud Agents auto-run all terminal commands. This matches the has_criteria of running a shell command and using its output as a supported, documented capability.
  • Partial Sandboxed / isolated execution environment
    Cursor documents full isolated-VM execution only for Cloud Agents: each cloud agent runs in its own isolated VM with a managed lifecycle, separate from the host machine. The default local/foreground Agent, however, runs directly on the user's machine; its Run Modes (e.g. Auto-review) only provide best-effort, per-command shell sandboxing 'when it can' and are explicitly described as guardrails rather than a hard security boundary. Because full sandboxed isolation is documented only for a specific cloud-hosted mode rather than as the default local execution environment, this matches the partial_criteria ("Sandboxing is available only in a specific plan or cloud-hosted mode").

  • Has Parallel independent task execution
    Cursor's Agents Window is documented as an agent-first workspace for managing multiple independent agent sessions concurrently across repos, worktrees, cloud, and remote environments; each tab/session is its own independent agent. The companion Worktrees feature lets each concurrently-running agent operate in its own isolated Git worktree, so independent tasks run truly in parallel rather than serially against a shared working directory. This is a documented, product-native mechanism for running multiple independent tasks concurrently, distinct from delegating parts of one task to coordinated sub-agents (which is out of scope per the exclusion for this feature).
  • Has Self-healing error recovery
    Cursor's Terminal docs state that the cloud agent auto-runs all terminal commands, letting it iterate on tests, in contrast to the foreground Agent which requires approval for every command.     Cursor's Checkpoints feature (in Agent chat) lets a user restore the full agent session's file state to any earlier point in the conversation in one operation, undoing every file change the Agent made since that point, not just a single file or hunk. This is a documented, session-wide restore mechanism distinct from per-hunk diff accept/reject, satisfying the has_criteria for session-wide checkpoint/rollback.

Agent Customization & Orchestration

  • Has Multi-agent / sub-agent orchestration
    Cursor documents multiple, complementary supported orchestration mechanisms: (1) subagents that a parent agent can delegate specific pieces of work to, each running in its own context window and returning results to the parent; (2) built-in parallel-agent support (Agents window / /multitask) that runs multiple agents simultaneously, each in an isolated git worktree with its own branch and files, to avoid conflicts; and (3) cloud/background agents that can run additional agent instances remotely and in parallel. Together these are a documented, supported delegation/parallel-coordination mechanism, matching has_criteria, not merely undocumented flags or the user manually running separate sessions.
  • Has User-defined sub-agent roles
    Cursor documents a file-based custom-subagent authoring mechanism: Markdown files with YAML frontmatter placed under .cursor/agents/, each defining the subagent's own name/description (persona and effective system prompt), a tools field that scopes which tools the subagent may call (or a readonly flag restricting it to read-only actions), and frontmatter that can also configure disallowed tools, MCP servers, hooks, max turns, skills, and background behavior. This is a documented, supported extension mechanism for authoring a new role with its own prompt and independently scoped tool access, going beyond the fixed built-in agent roles, and matches the has_criteria.

  • Has Custom tool / function-calling API

This is a documented API/config surface for registering a callable function/tool that does not require the developer to build or wire in an external MCP server, matching has_criteria; it is scoped to the Cursor SDK (for building custom agent-powered applications) rather than a setting inside the standard IDE chat/agent UI.

  • Has Agent lifecycle hooks
    Cursor documents a native hooks mechanism configured via .cursor/hooks.json (repo-scoped) or ~/.cursor/hooks.json (user-scoped) that runs user-supplied shell commands at defined points across the agent's action lifecycle: beforeShellExecution, afterShellExecution, beforeReadFile, afterFileEdit, preToolUse, postToolUse, postToolUseFailure, subagentStart, subagentStop, and preCompact. A hook receives a JSON payload on stdin and can print a JSON permission decision (allow/deny/ask) on stdout, or use exit code 2 to block the action, satisfying the requirement that hooks can influence/block (not just passively observe) the agent's action. Coverage spans pre/post tool-call and shell-execution events generally, not a single narrow lifecycle point, so this exceeds the partial_criteria ceiling.
