Per Cursor's own announcements, the catalog was expanded with 'over 30 new plugins' from named partners including Atlassian, Datadog, GitLab, Glean, Hugging Face, monday.com, and PlanetScale, in addition to earlier launch partners such as Amplitude, AWS, Figma, Linear, and Stripe. This is well beyond the 1-2 integrations that would only qualify as partial, and the catalog is hosted and curated directly by the vendor (plugins are reviewed/audited before listing), so it is not the kind of unendorsed community marketplace excluded by the taxonomy criteria. This satisfies the has_criteria of an official catalog listing supported third-party integrations.
  • Has Mobile app access
    Cursor for iOS is officially documented as a native iPhone app (public beta, on all paid plans) that provides direct access to the assistant: launching and controlling coding agents, voice input, model selection, and reviewing/merging PRs from the phone, not merely account management or a responsive web view. An official Android native app was not found; Android access relies on the web dashboard (cursor.com/agents) or installing it as a PWA, which is a documented but lesser-tier access path. Since the has_criteria is satisfied by an official app on iOS or Android and the iOS app provides genuine assistant access, this is recorded as has, with the iOS-only native scope noted as a constraint.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Headless / non-interactive CI mode
    Cursor's official CLI documentation describes a dedicated headless/non-interactive mode (`-p`/`--print`) intended for scripting and automation, with a documented `--output-format json` / `--output-format stream-json` machine-readable output mode and documented shell exit-code semantics (checking `$?` to detect success/failure), and GitHub Actions integration for CI/CD. This combination of non-interactive invocation, structured output, and documented exit codes meets the has_criteria for a headless CI mode.
  • Not found Full offline operation
    No official Cursor source states that the whole product (core AI functionality plus surrounding product operation) functions with zero network connectivity. Cursor's own documentation and enterprise/pricing pages describe network-dependent architecture: an official Network Configuration doc covers proxy configuration, IP allowlisting, and required outbound connectivity (not an offline mode); Cursor's changelog documents 'self-hosted' Cloud Agents that keep code and tool execution on infrastructure the customer controls, but this is a deployment-location option for the agent runtime, not a fully-disconnected/air-gapped operating mode, and it still depends on network connectivity between components. The pricing page (cursor.com/pricing) and the enterprise page describe plan tiers, SSO, audit logs, and cloud-based security/compliance controls, with no mention of offline or air-gapped operation. No changelog entry, docs page, product page, or pricing page claims zero-network operation. All relevant source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing) were checked via targeted searches with no unresolved access gaps; the searches consistently surfaced only network-dependent architecture and user requests for offline/air-gapped support that Cursor has not (per these official pages) fulfilled.

Security & Governance

  • Has Enterprise SSO / access control
    Cursor documents SAML 2.0 SSO (supporting Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace and others, plus SCIM provisioning and enforced SSO/disabled local login) and fine-grained RBAC covering organizations, teams and agents, on Teams and Enterprise plans.
    plan_or_license
  • Has Data retention / training opt-out controls
    Cursor documents a customer-facing 'Privacy Mode' setting; when enabled, customer data is not used for training by Cursor and model providers will not store or train on the data, backed by zero-data-retention agreements with model providers.
  • Partial On-premises / private cloud deployment
    Cursor documents a Self-Hosted Pool (and a Self-Hosted Cloud Run variant on Google Cloud) that lets Enterprise customers run Cloud Agent worker processes inside their own company-managed infrastructure, keeping repos, build caches, secrets, and tool execution inside the customer's network. However, the same official docs and blog post explicitly state that the agent loop, orchestration, and model inference remain in Cursor's cloud even when Self-Hosted Pool is used, and this option is scoped specifically to the asynchronous Cloud Agent feature rather than the product as a whole -- the core editor, chat, and Tab completion are not documented as deployable on-premises. This is a genuine, officially documented private/customer-infrastructure execution option for one feature, but falls short of on-premises deployment of the full service, matching the partial_criteria's spirit of private deployment limited to a narrower scope than the whole product.
    other plan_or_license
  • Partial IP indemnity / public-code duplication filter
    Cursor's Master Services Agreement (the negotiated contract used for organizations with a signed Order Form, i.e. Enterprise-tier customers) contains a stated IP indemnification commitment: Anysphere indemnifies the Customer against third-party claims that the Service or a Suggestion infringes or misappropriates third-party IP rights, subject to standard carve-outs (customer disabled safety/content filters, customer knew or should have known the Suggestion was likely infringing, or customer lacked lawful rights over the Customer Data used to generate the Suggestion). This appears tied to organizations with a negotiated MSA rather than to the standard individual Free/Pro Terms of Service, under which the indemnification flows the other way (customer indemnifies Anysphere). Checks of cursor.com's documentation (cursor.com/docs), product/security pages (cursor.com, cursor.com/security), pricing (cursor.com/pricing), changelog (cursor.com/changelog), and blog (cursor.com/blog) found no description of a configurable filter that blocks code suggestions matching public code, comparable to GitHub Copilot's 'duplication detection filter'. Community forum threads on forum.cursor.com show users repeatedly asking whether Cursor offers such a filter, with no confirmation from Cursor of such a feature. Per the feature's partial_criteria, only one of the two qualifying mechanisms (the IP indemnification commitment) is documented, and that mechanism itself is restricted to a specific commercial arrangement (negotiated Enterprise MSA), so status is partial rather than has or not_found.
    plan_or_license other
  • Has Audit logging & usage metrics
    Cursor documents an admin-accessible Audit Log covering 19 event types (security changes, rule/asset edits, configuration updates), viewable in the web dashboard and exportable as CSV. This is documented as an Enterprise-plan feature per the official pricing page.
    plan_or_license
  • Partial Local / offline (BYO) model support
    Cursor's official documentation confirms a documented mechanism for pointing the tool at a customer-controlled model endpoint rather than only Cursor's own cloud-hosted models: Settings > Models exposes an 'Override OpenAI Base URL' option for a custom model, and Cursor's own enterprise documentation states that a custom model reached via an OpenAI-compatible base URL override (or a third-party gateway) carries the region of that gateway/model - confirming this custom-model path is an officially documented, supported mechanism rather than an unsupported workaround. Because self-hosted local inference backends such as Ollama expose an OpenAI-compatible API, this documented base URL override is the supported way community guides use to run Cursor against a self-hosted/local model. However, this falls short of full 'has' status: Cursor's own documentation and independent reporting consistently indicate the custom-model endpoint must be reachable over the network (a public URL or gateway), because Cursor's backend participates in the request path rather than the client connecting directly to a purely local/offline endpoint - so a strictly air-gapped, localhost-only model is not directly supported without exposing it. Cursor also does not market or document this generically as 'local model support' (e.g. no dedicated Ollama/local-model documentation page was found); the local-model use is a documented-mechanism-plus-community-application rather than a first-class, explicitly named local/offline model feature. This combination of a real but narrower/constrained supported path meets partial_criteria rather than has_criteria or not_found.
    other region
  • Has Secret detection & redaction
    Cursor's official 'LLM Safety and Controls' documentation describes automatic, multi-stage detection and blocking/redaction of secrets: prompts are scanned for sensitive data before submission to LLMs and blocked if they contain API keys/credentials, PII, or proprietary information; files are scanned before the agent reads them, with redaction or blocking of access to configuration files containing secrets; and generated code is scanned before being written to disk, including checks for API keys and credentials in the generated output. This covers detection and redaction/blocking both before content reaches the model and before it is written to disk, satisfying the has_criteria and going beyond a narrow fixed-pattern warn-only mechanism.

  • Has Agent network egress control / firewall
    Cursor's cloud/background agent sandbox lets a customer define exactly which domains the agent may reach via a sandbox.json allow-list, with three configurable levels of network access (restrict to your allow-list, allow-list plus Cursor defaults, or unrestricted). Enterprise admins can additionally enforce organization-wide network allow-lists/deny-lists from the admin dashboard, applying egress policy to all agent sandbox sessions.
    plan_or_license

    Cursor's documented default is US-only data residency (inference, processing, and storage). EU + Iceland inference-only coverage exists but only 'on request' via enterprise enrollment with the account team, and broader EU support/additional regions are described as still 'in active development' rather than a generally available, self-service, per-customer region guarantee.

  • Has Sub-processor / third-party data-sharing disclosure
    Cursor's Data Processing Addendum states that for commercial uses where Anysphere (Cursor's operating company) acts as a data processor, sub-processors can be reviewed at a dedicated, vendor-maintained Trust Center page (trust.cursor.com/subprocessors), with 30 business days' prior written notice given for new sub-processors or changes, posted at the same URL. This is a published, itemized, vendor-maintained sub-processor disclosure that is publicly accessible, satisfying the has_criteria.
  • Has Data Processing Agreement (DPA) availability
    Anysphere publishes a standing Data Processing Addendum (DPA) on its terms site, incorporated into the Master Services Agreement, governing its processing of customer personal data. It is publicly posted rather than gated to a specific enterprise tier.

    Cursor's official security page explicitly states data is encrypted both at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+).

Additional facts

Built-in tools

  • Named sub-agents:

    Beyond the general-purpose Agent, Cursor documents several distinct, named built-in agent roles: Bugbot (an automated pull-request reviewer, with a companion Autofix capability that spawns cloud agents to propose fixes for issues it finds) and a pair of always-on Security Agents - a Security Reviewer that checks every pull request for security vulnerabilities, and a Vulnerability Scanner that runs scheduled scans of the codebase for known vulnerabilities and outdated dependencies. Cursor also supports authoring fully custom subagents as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter under .cursor/agents/, each with its own name/description, an independently scoped tools allowlist or read-only flag, and optional MCP servers, hooks, and skills.

    • “Bugbot reviews pull requests and identifies bugs, security issues, and code quality problems.”
    • “Cursor offers two types of always-on security agents: Security Reviewer and Vulnerability Scanner”
    • “Subagents are specialized AI assistants that Cursor's agent can delegate tasks to. Each subagent operates in its own context window, handles specific types of work, and returns its result to the parent agent.”

Pricing & licensing

  • Pricing tiers:

    Cursor's individual plans are Hobby (free, limited included usage, no credit card required), Pro ($20/month, $16/month billed annually, with a $20 included monthly credit pool), Pro+ ($60/month, ~$70 included usage), and Ultra ($200/month, ~$400 included usage, priority feature access). Team plans are billed per seat: a Standard Teams tier at $40/seat/month and a Premium Teams tier at $120/seat/month, with Enterprise custom-priced and pooled across an organization. All paid individual/team plans include unlimited Tab completions, access to all models, Cloud Agents, and Bugbot; Teams additionally adds the admin dashboard, centralized billing, and SSO. Annual billing is documented as saving 20% versus monthly billing on paid plans.

    • “Hobby: Free with limited included API usage. Pro: $20/month with $20 included API usage. Pro+: $60/month with $70 included API usage. Ultra: $200/month with $400 included API usage. Teams Standard: $40 per seat per month. Teams Premium: $120 per seat per month. All paid plans include unlimited Tab completions, all models, Cloud Agents, and Bugbot; Teams adds admin dashboard, centralized billing, and SSO.”

Security & data handling

  • Data usage:

    Cursor's official security page states that data is encrypted at rest (AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+), and that Cursor maintains zero-data-retention agreements with all model providers; an opt-in 'Privacy Mode' setting ensures customer data is not used for training by Cursor or by model providers. Cursor separately states SOC 2 Type II compliance (with an attestation report available on request via its Trust Center) on SOC 2 Type II-compliant AWS infrastructure, and states compliance with GDPR and CCPA requirements. A standing Data Processing Addendum governs Anysphere's processing of customer personal data, with an itemized sub-processor list published at trust.cursor.com/subprocessors and 30 business days' notice for sub-processor changes.

    • “Cursor employs industry-standard encryption protocols to ensure that personal data is encrypted at rest and in transit. ... Cursor uses AES-256 encryption at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit. ... Cursor offers zero data retention and maintains zero data retention agreements with all model providers.”

    • “The Data Processing Addendum (DPA) governs Anysphere, Inc.'s processing of Personal Data provided by customers through the Service, in accordance with the Master Services Agreement between Anysphere and the Customer.”

Extensibility & MCP ecosystem

  • Extensibility via MCP:

    Cursor's primary open extension point is the Model Context Protocol (MCP): MCP servers connect the agent to external tools and data sources (e.g. Google Drive, Notion, databases, other APIs) and are configured consistently across both the editor and the CLI. An official, vendor-curated Marketplace (cursor.com/marketplace) lists more than 30 third-party MCP servers/plugins from named partners such as Atlassian, Datadog, GitLab, Glean, Hugging Face, monday.com, and PlanetScale, alongside earlier launch partners including Amplitude, AWS, Figma, Linear, and Stripe. For organizations, a documented 'Team MCP' mechanism lets admins configure MCP servers once from Dashboard -> Integrations & MCP and distribute them across cloud agents, the Agents Window, the IDE, and the CLI, with a governed Team Marketplace supporting both SCIM directory-group and organization-group-based access control, so individual developers do not need to configure MCP servers themselves.

devin

Stale · researched 2026-07-25T21:38:50Z

Characteristics

Devin is Cognition's autonomous AI software engineering agent: rather than a chat-based coding assistant, it is designed for asynchronous task delegation, where a user or ticket describes a piece of work and Devin plans, implements, tests, and delivers it with minimal supervision. Cloud-hosted Devin sessions run inside an isolated sandboxed compute environment (a Linux VM) with their own shell, file system, editor, and browser, letting the agent run commands, edit multiple files, and browse the web as part of completing a task. Devin monitors its own terminal and build output, self-correcting on compiler errors and test failures without a new prompt, and produces a full session timeline (commands, diffs, browser actions) that supports checkpoint-based rollback of both files and memory. It supports natural-language task specification, image/screenshot- and Figma-driven UI work, and can run many independent sessions - including manager/worker "MultiDevin" fan-out - in parallel or on a recurring schedule.

Access methods

Devin is reached primarily through a hosted web application (app.devin.ai), where Free, Pro, Max, and Teams self-serve plans can sign up directly; Enterprise access (including private/VPC deployment) is arranged through Sales. Beyond the web app, Cognition ships Devin CLI ("Devin for Terminal"), an official standalone local coding agent installed via a shell/PowerShell script, and Devin Desktop (the rebranded Windsurf editor, now shipping a Devin Local agent alongside cloud sessions). IDE reach is extended through a beta first-party VS Code extension and JetBrains support delivered via JetBrains' Agent Client Protocol (ACP) rather than a native plugin. Devin can also be triggered from Slack, a GitHub issue, or a connected Jira/Linear ticket, and automated/headless invocation is supported for CI/CD pipelines via API tokens or the COGNITION_API_KEY environment variable in place of interactive OAuth2 login. No official first-party mobile (iOS/Android) application was found on any checked Cognition or Devin domain.

Internal tools and mechanisms

Devin's session toolkit lets it operate its shell, editor, and browser concurrently (e.g. reading several files while a command runs), and once a repository is indexed it gains Ask Devin (natural-language Q&A grounded in the repo), DeepWiki (auto-generated architecture wikis), and, in Devin Desktop, the Fast Context subagent for rapid whole-codebase retrieval. Interactive Planning has Devin produce and expose a citation-backed plan for review - optionally gated behind an explicit "wait for approval" - before autonomous execution starts, and a tiered permission system (Devin CLI's Normal / Accept Edits / Bypass / Autonomous modes, or the cloud product's Agency setting) governs how much user confirmation is required for writes, shell commands, and network access. Knowledge provides persistent, automatically-recalled project/organization memory, and a layered instruction-precedence model (personal AGENTS.local.md, project AGENTS.md, and non-overridable organization/enterprise settings) resolves conflicting guidance. Devin CLI additionally exposes lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PermissionRequest) that can block, modify, or add context to a tool call, and Subagents that let a parent session delegate sub-tasks to built-in profiles (subagent_explore, subagent_general) or user-authored custom profiles.

Workflows and use cases

Devin's default output is git-native: after connecting a GitHub, GitLab, or GitHub Enterprise Server repository, it clones the repo, works on a branch, and opens a pull request as a contributing teammate, with Devin Review adding an automated first-pass review layer (bug/security flags, optional auto-fix suggestions applied from the diff view) between generation and human review. Devin generates unit/integration tests on request (vendor guidance cites roughly 60-70% baseline unit-test coverage from typical usage), and documented automation templates run scheduled dependency/CVE scanning (npm audit, pip-audit, cargo audit, trivy) and respond to static-analysis findings (SonarQube, Fortify, Veracode) surfaced through CI/CD. A recurring, dedicated use case is large-scale legacy modernization and refactoring (e.g. COBOL/Fortran/.NET/Perl migrations), which can be fanned out across many parallel "MultiDevin" worker sessions for repeated, isolated jobs like migrations or lint clean-ups. Scheduled Sessions support one-time or cron-based recurring runs, and tasks can be delegated asynchronously via Slack, a GitHub issue, or a Jira/Linear ticket, with Devin reporting back once work is complete.

Integrations

Devin's Integrations Overview documents native, first-party connections to platforms including GitHub, Slack, Jira, and Linear, alongside a built-in Secrets Manager for storing credentials Devin can use. Broader third-party reach is delivered through a first-party MCP (Model Context Protocol) Marketplace (Settings > Connections), supporting stdio, SSE, and HTTP transports and documented as connecting Devin to hundreds of external tools and data sources (official examples include Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Notion, Airtable, and Stripe); organization admins can add custom MCP servers and enforce an org-wide allowlist. IDE-side integration extends to a beta VS Code extension and JetBrains support via the Agent Client Protocol.

Security

Cognition documents a formal Data Processing Addendum (with SCCs/UK Addendum for cross-border transfer) and states in its Enterprise Terms of Service that it will indemnify customers against third-party IP-infringement claims arising from the Services. Enterprise security documentation states all data transmission is encrypted in transit and at rest, backed by a SOC 2 Type II certification and a gated (NDA-access) SafeBase Trust Center that includes sub-processor disclosures - sub-processor use and 15-day change-notice obligations are documented in the DPA, though no directly public itemized sub-processor list was found. Paid-plan customers can opt out of model training via a Data Controls page (which also enables Zero Data Retention with model providers), and Enterprise customers have a contractual no-training-without-consent commitment. Enterprise-tier access controls include SSO/SCIM via SAML or OIDC identity providers with group-based RBAC, and a dedicated enterprise audit-logs API endpoint. Network egress from Devin CLI's sandboxed execution can be restricted via an admin-configurable, organization-authoritative domain allowlist/denylist. Deployment options beyond shared multi-tenant SaaS include a single-tenant VPC "Customer Dedicated Deployment" and Devin Outposts (customer-controlled execution infrastructure reachable over outbound HTTPS only); in both cases Devin's reasoning "Brain" continues to run in Cognition's own cloud.

Constraints

Several of Devin's most consequential controls are Enterprise-tier only: SSO/SCIM and RBAC, the audit-logs API, Customer Dedicated Deployment/VPC hosting, non-overridable organization-level Knowledge/instruction settings, and enterprise-managed secrets, MCP allowlisting, and build pinning. A number of mechanisms are documented specifically for Devin CLI ("Devin for Terminal") - lifecycle hooks, the four-mode permission system, and user-defined custom subagents - and are not confirmed for the cloud-hosted web session product, which instead exposes a simpler Agency autonomy setting. IDE coverage is uneven: the VS Code extension is explicitly a beta feature, and JetBrains support runs through JetBrains' own Agent Client Protocol rather than a native Cognition-built plugin. Even where execution moves onto customer-controlled infrastructure (VPC deployment or Devin Outposts), the reasoning "Brain" always runs in Cognition's multi-tenant cloud, so no fully offline or air-gapped operating mode is documented. Some frequently-asked capabilities remain unresolved from official sources alone: whether Devin supports a non-MCP custom tool/function-registration API, whether it supports customer-supplied local/self-hosted models in place of Cognition's curated model roster, and whether it automatically detects/redacts secrets appearing in its own output are all marked uncertain rather than confirmed, and no official first-party mobile app was located.

Use cases

  • Automated first-pass pull request review Documented

    Devin Review runs an automated quality pass on pull requests - flagging bugs, security issues, and conformance problems, and optionally proposing auto-fixes a human can accept directly from the diff view - before a human reviewer looks at the change.

    • “Devin Review provides automated first-pass reviews on pull requests, checking for correctness and conformance with organizational best practices.”

    Why inferred: This combines three independently documented capabilities - headless CI/CD invocation via environment-variable authentication, scheduled/CVE dependency scanning automation templates, and CI-triggered static-analysis remediation - into a single continuous pipeline use case that no single official page describes end-to-end as one named workflow.

    integration_required

Agentic Execution & Runtime

  • Has Autonomous multi-step task execution
    Devin's official introduction documentation describes it as an autonomous AI software engineer that operates inside its own sandboxed compute environment (shell, editor, browser) to plan and execute multi-step tasks - running commands, editing files, and testing its own work - without requiring step-by-step user confirmation, and reporting back on completion.
  • Has Background / long-running task execution
    Devin is documented as an asynchronous task-delegation agent: the user assigns a task (via the IDE, Slack, or API) and Devin continues working independently in the background without occupying the user's active session, optionally sending a private Slack message whenever the run reaches a status update.
    integration_required
  • Has Terminal command execution
    Devin executes shell/terminal commands directly as a documented, supported capability of both the cloud agent and the Devin CLI. The CLI documents four built-in permission modes (Normal, Accept Edits, Bypass, Autonomous) that govern how much user confirmation is required before a command runs.
    other
  • Has Sandboxed / isolated execution environment
    Vendor documentation states that cloud-hosted Devin sessions run generated code and shell commands inside an isolated cloud compute sandbox (a Linux/Ubuntu VM) rather than directly on the user's machine, and the Devin CLI separately exposes a --sandbox flag selecting an OS-enforced Autonomous permission mode.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Parallel independent task execution
    Official Devin guidance documents running multiple independent Devin sessions concurrently as a supported workflow, including delegating to 'managed Devins' that launch and run many scoped, independent sessions in parallel from a single coordinating session or the Devin API.
  • Has Self-healing error recovery
    Devin's documentation describes autonomously monitoring its own terminal/build output after a change: on a compiler error, it parses the stack trace, opens the offending file, corrects the line, and re-runs the build command, iterating on the failure without a new user prompt.
  • Has Agent session checkpoint & rollback
    Cognition's official product-update documentation describes a session-wide checkpoint/rollback mechanism: Devin records a full timeline of a session (commands, diffs, browser actions), and restoring a checkpoint rolls back both Devin's files (in the sandbox) and its memory to that earlier point, not just a single file or hunk.
  • Has Scheduled / recurring task execution
    Devin documents a native Scheduled Sessions mechanism letting users configure a one-time future run or a recurring, cron-expression-based schedule that starts a Devin session automatically, without an active user session initiating it at that moment.

Agent Customization & Orchestration

  • Has Multi-agent / sub-agent orchestration
    Devin CLI's documented Subagents mechanism lets the main agent spawn independent worker agents to handle sub-tasks - sharing tools and codebase context with the parent while operating in their own conversation chain - and explicitly supports running such delegated work (e.g. exploring a codebase, running tests, implementing a feature) in parallel or in the background. The agent can select from built-in profiles (e.g. subagent_general, explore subagents) or user-defined custom profiles when delegating, and the mechanism supports spawning multiple or nested subagents for a single larger task, matching the requirement that delegation to sub-agents/parallel agent instances be a documented, supported mechanism.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has User-defined sub-agent roles
    Devin CLI documents a mechanism for authoring custom subagent profiles: Markdown/YAML-frontmatter files placed under the .devin/agents/ (project) or user-config directory, with fields for name, description, model, and allowed-tools (independent tool scoping). Once defined, custom profiles appear alongside Devin's built-in subagent profiles (e.g. subagent_explore, subagent_general) and the parent agent can select or be directed to a specific named profile when delegating a sub-task, meeting the requirement for a documented, user-authored role with its own prompt and tool scope.
    platform_or_ide
  • Uncertain Custom tool / function-calling API
    This repair pass checked all D-009-relevant source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing) plus integration_catalog for Devin's extensibility model, but this worker session had no WebFetch tool available, so official pages could only be approached through WebSearch's AI-generated summaries rather than direct, verbatim page fetches. Those summaries consistently describe Devin's CLI extensibility surface (docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility and its Skills / Custom Subagents / Hooks / MCP Servers sub-pages) as offering: Skills (Markdown workflow prompts with YAML frontmatter, not a callable-function API), Custom Subagents (delegated worker profiles), Hooks (shell/LLM commands fired at lifecycle events), and MCP Servers, which the docs summary explicitly frames as the mechanism that 'provide[s] entirely new tools the agent can call.' A follow-up query on the project configuration page (docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/configuration) returned config.json as covering only MCP server definitions and permissions -- no separate custom-tool schema -- which does not corroborate an earlier, less precise search result that mentioned a '.devin/config.yaml' file for 'custom tools'; that earlier claim could not be reproduced or confirmed and was not relied on. The changelog (docs.devin.ai/release-notes and docs.devin.ai/desktop/changelog, via search) mentions a 'Devin plugin system for extending Devin Local' (preview, opt-in for enterprises) described only as letting teams extend Devin 'with the tools, skills, and plugins your team already uses,' alongside a note that 'subagents can now call MCP tools directly' -- too vague, and too centered on MCP/skills, to confirm or deny a distinct native function-registration API. The pricing page (devin.ai/pricing) and product page (devin.ai) surfaced no official statements on this feature at all in search results; only third-party review sites came back for those queries. Because the only verbatim-confirmable official framing found (extensibility overview + configuration page) points to MCP as the sole mechanism for adding new callable tools, but the plugin-system changelog mention is genuinely ambiguous and could not be checked against source text directly, and because the lack of WebFetch access is itself an access gap on every one of these official pages, this is marked uncertain rather than not_found or has/partial, per the repair guidance to not attach positive evidence to a not_found/uncertain verdict when verification is incomplete.
  • Has Agent lifecycle hooks
    Devin CLI documents a lifecycle-hooks mechanism (configured via .devin/hooks.v1.json) where user-supplied hook scripts fire at defined points in the agent's action lifecycle - including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, and PermissionRequest - and can block, modify, or add context to a tool call before it executes. Rewritten arguments returned by a hook are merged into the tool call so the agent executes the updated action instead of the original, satisfying the requirement that hooks can influence, not just passively observe, the action. The official changelog corroborates ongoing hook capability expansion (e.g. richer stdin tool information, prompt-blocking repairs) across CLI and IDE integrations, indicating this is a maintained, general-purpose mechanism rather than a single narrow event type.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Permission / autonomy-level granularity
    Devin CLI documents a tiered permission system with (at minimum) four distinct, independently selectable modes covering different action categories: Normal Mode auto-approves read-only operations while requiring explicit approval for writes and shell commands; Accept Edits Mode auto-approves in-workspace file edits while still prompting for shell commands and out-of-workspace writes; Bypass Mode auto-approves all tool calls; and Autonomous Mode auto-approves shell commands/network fetches under OS-level sandbox enforcement. Approvals can additionally be scoped once/session/permanently-per-project, and organization admins can enforce deny/ask rules via Team Settings that remain active regardless of the user's selected mode. This goes beyond a single global confirm/auto-run toggle and meets the requirement for configurable, per-action-category permission levels.
    other platform_or_ide
  • Has Plan visibility before execution
    Devin's documented Interactive Planning workflow has Devin investigate the repository and produce a detailed plan - including code citations/snippets and file scope - before autonomous execution begins. Documentation instructs the user to review the plan for wrong files, misunderstood requirements, unnecessary steps, or out-of-scope changes, and to edit the plan or give feedback before Devin proceeds; for complex tasks the user can explicitly require Devin to "Wait for my approval" on the complete plan prior to execution. This matches the requirement that the tool show an upfront plan/step list for review before autonomous execution starts.

Context & Code Quality

  • Has Codebase-wide semantic search
    Once a repository is indexed, Devin supports Ask Devin (natural-language Q&A grounded in the indexed repo) and DeepWiki (auto-generated architecture diagrams/summaries with links to source), and Devin Desktop's Fast Context subagent retrieves relevant code from the whole codebase using an optimized retrieval-augmented approach rather than plain text matching. Together these document meaning-based retrieval ranked by relevance across the whole indexed project, not just the open file.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Large-repository / long-context handling
    Devin documents specific mechanisms for large repositories and long sessions rather than relying on raw model context size alone: an optimized retrieval-augmented (RAG) context engine plus the Fast Context subagent for rapid whole-codebase retrieval, a .devin/wiki.json configuration for repositories large enough to hit built-in wiki-generation limits, and context-window management in Devin Desktop's Cascade (occasional summarization and history clearing, with a usage indicator) once a session's context grows long.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Persistent project memory / custom instructions
    Knowledge is a documented, dedicated mechanism for storing tips, conventions, and organizational context that persists across all future sessions and is automatically recalled (via a trigger description) without needing to re-enter the same instructions in every prompt, satisfying the has_criteria for a persistent, automatically-applied project memory mechanism.
  • Has Automated test generation
    Devin documentation describes generating unit and integration tests for existing or new code on request, including via @ Mention prompts targeting specific functions/files, with documented prompt templates for coverage and edge-case generation. Vendor guidance also quantifies typical coverage (60-70% of unit tests with basic usage), indicating this is a supported, documented capability rather than incidental code generation.
  • Has Automated code review / PR review
    Devin Review is a dedicated, documented automated PR-review workflow (also usable from a local CLI) that runs a first-pass review of a diff/PR, flags bugs and security issues, and can auto-fix detected issues. GitHub Commit Status Checks surface review progress directly on the PR, and a separate Windsurf/Cascade PR-review capability exists for Teams/Enterprise. This goes beyond ad hoc chat review, so it meets the has_criteria for a dedicated automated code review/PR review workflow.
    integration_required
  • Has Static analysis / linting integration
    Devin documents CI/CD integration in which findings from static-analysis/SAST tools (SonarQube, Fortify, Veracode) are surfaced to Devin, which reviews and can automatically fix flagged issues; Devin Review's own Bug Catcher/lint findings likewise feed into its automated review and Auto-Fix suggestions rather than being displayed only for humans. This is a documented feedback loop from static analysis into AI-driven suggestions/fixes, not just editor-side lint display.
    integration_required
  • Has Dependency vulnerability scanning (SCA)
    Devin's documented automation templates scan project dependencies against GitHub Security Advisories and CVE databases: the Dependency Vulnerability Scanner correlates findings with severity/fix recommendations, and the Security Vulnerability Scan runs ecosystem scanners (npm audit, pip-audit, cargo audit, trivy) weekly, cross-references results against known CVEs, files tickets, and can auto-open patch PRs. Devin Review additionally has a built-in, default-enabled Security scan section. This is a documented integration with a CVE/vulnerability database whose findings are surfaced for the project's dependencies.
    integration_required
  • Has Layered instruction precedence (personal/repository/organization)
    Devin documents at least three distinct instruction/configuration scopes with an automatically-applied precedence order: a personal/global scope (~/.config/devin/AGENTS.md and AGENTS.local.md for personal, unshared preferences), a repository/project scope (AGENTS.md files, resolved with nearest-file-in-directory-tree precedence so subdirectory files override the project root, which overrides the global user config), and an organization/enterprise scope for shared settings, where documentation states organization-level (enterprise) settings can never be overridden by project or user config. This meets the has_criteria of at least two documented scopes with a defined, automatically-applied precedence order (here, three scopes).
    plan_or_license

Workflow & Ecosystem

  • Has Native git workflow support
    Devin's standard workflow is git-native: after a GitHub/GitLab (or GitHub Enterprise Server) repository is connected via Settings > Integrations, Devin clones the repo into its session, works on branches, commits changes, and participates as a contributor (pushing branches, opening/responding to pull requests). Git is documented as Devin's primary output channel.
    integration_required
  • Has Pull request creation
    Devin's documented GitHub integration explicitly enables it to create pull requests (and respond to PR comments) as its primary output for completed work, following any PR template present in the connected repository.
    integration_required
  • Has Multi-IDE / multi-editor support
    Devin is not limited to a single IDE. Cognition publishes an official VS Code extension (in the CognitionAI GitHub org) that works in VS Code and VS Code-based forks, letting a developer hand off async work, check out Devin's PRs, and review a 'Global Diff' locally. Separately, Devin integrates with JetBrains IDEs through JetBrains' built-in Agent Client Protocol (ACP) support, installable straight from the ACP Registry or configurable as a custom ACP agent backed by the Devin CLI. Devin Desktop (the rebranded Windsurf editor Cognition now ships) provides a further dedicated IDE surface.
    platform_or_ide
  • Has Standalone CLI access
    Cognition ships an official standalone command-line tool, Devin CLI ('Devin for Terminal'), installed via a shell/PowerShell install script from cli.devin.ai, that gives developers a terminal interface to trigger Devin runs, manage files, and automate tasks from the command line as a local coding agent with access to the local codebase, tools, and environment (while still connecting to Devin's cloud services for authentication/model execution).
  • Has Web-hosted / browser access
    Devin is documented as a cloud-hosted product: users sign up and operate it through a web interface at app.devin.ai, where it opens a sandboxed cloud environment (shell, editor, browser) and can also be invoked via Slack or a GitHub issue. The official product/pricing pages confirm self-serve Individual and Teams plans are provisioned through this hosted web app, distinct from any local/desktop client.
    plan_or_license
  • Has MCP / plugin extensibility
    Devin documents a first-party MCP (Model Context Protocol) marketplace, supporting stdio, SSE, and HTTP transports, that lets Devin connect to third-party tools and data sources (e.g. Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Notion, Airtable, Stripe) configurable from Settings > Connections > MCP servers in the Devin web app.
  • Has Third-party integration catalog
    Devin's official Integrations Overview documentation describes a dedicated catalog of native integrations (GitHub, Slack, Jira, Linear, and others) plus a Secrets Manager for credentials and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) Marketplace in Settings for connecting to hundreds of additional external tools and data sources. This constitutes a documented, first-party third-party integration catalog rather than a single hard-coded connector.

Security & Governance

  • Has Enterprise SSO / access control
    Devin documents Enterprise-tier SSO via SAML/OIDC (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Duo, PingID, or any SAML/OIDC-compliant IdP) together with SCIM provisioning and group-based role assignment (RBAC), satisfying has_criteria for enterprise SSO plus role/permission management.

    Devin documents a customer-facing Data Controls settings page where paid-plan customers can opt out of having their data used for model training, which also enables Zero Data Retention with model providers. This is a concrete, actionable control, satisfying has_criteria.
    plan_or_license
  • Has On-premises / private cloud deployment
    Cognition documents deployment options beyond a standard shared-tenant SaaS cloud. 'Customer Dedicated Deployment' hosts Devin in an auto-scaling, customer-isolated environment inside a single-tenant VPC reachable via AWS PrivateLink or an IPSec tunnel - a dedicated private-cloud instance distinct from the shared Enterprise Cloud. Separately, 'Devin Outposts' (announced 2026-07-21) lets the execution environment (the Devbox: shell, file edits, repository access) run entirely on infrastructure the customer operates - a workstation, GPU server, VM inside a private network, Kubernetes cluster, or Apple silicon Mac - requiring only outbound HTTPS with no inbound ports or VPN tunnel. Additional facts

Built-in tools

  • Named sub-agents:

    Devin CLI's Subagents mechanism ships with built-in named worker profiles that the parent agent selects automatically or on request: subagent_explore, a cheaper, fixed-model profile used for research/codebase-understanding subtasks, and subagent_general, used for subtasks that make code changes and which always runs on the same model the user selected for the parent session. Users can also author their own custom subagent profiles (name, description, model, allowed-tools) under .devin/agents/ alongside these built-in roles.

    • “Subagents let the main agent spawn independent workers to handle subtasks.”

Pricing & licensing

  • Plans and tiers:

    Devin's self-serve pricing is structured as a Free tier, a Pro plan (billed monthly, entry-level paid tier), a higher-usage Max plan, and a Teams plan (a per-organization base fee plus a per-seat fee for each full developer seat); Enterprise is quote-gated through Sales. Self-serve plans run on a token-based usage quota that refreshes on a schedule, while Enterprise billing is expressed in Agent Compute Units (ACUs) - a normalized measure of the virtual-machine time, model inference, and networking bandwidth Devin consumes per task, with roughly one ACU equating to about 15 minutes of active Devin work. Usage beyond a plan's included allowance is billed as additional consumption on top of the subscription.

    • “Self-serve plans can be signed up for directly at app.devin.ai.”
    • “An ACU (Agent Compute Unit) is a normalized measure of the computing resources Devin uses to complete a task, such as virtual machine time, model inference, and networking bandwidth.”

Security & data handling

  • Data usage:

    Cognition holds a SOC 2 Type II certification underpinning Devin's enterprise security posture, publishes a gated Trust Center (SafeBase-hosted, access by request plus NDA) covering compliance documentation and sub-processor listings, and states that all data transmission is encrypted both in transit and at rest.

    • “All data transmission is encrypted in transit and at rest.”
    • “To access the documentation on Cognition's Trust Center, you need to request access via a banner on the site... sign an NDA in the portal.”

Extensibility & MCP ecosystem

  • Extensibility via MCP:

    Devin ships a first-party MCP (Model Context Protocol) Marketplace, configurable from Settings > Connections in the web app, supporting stdio, SSE, and HTTP transports. It is documented as letting Devin connect to hundreds of external tools and data sources (examples cited in official documentation include Sentry, Datadog, Linear, Notion, Airtable, and Stripe), and organization admins can add custom/private MCP servers and enforce an org-wide MCP server allowlist.

    • “MCP is an open protocol that enables Devin to use hundreds of external tools and data sources.”
    • “Browse the MCP Marketplace in Settings to enable integrations with various tools.”
